tec-ngfw.summary: A firewall that decides which traffic may pass by application, user and content, not only by port, and blocks known attacks on the way.
tec-ngfw.protects: Internet edge, data centre and branch networks; stops scanning, exploit attempts, malware downloads and command-and-control traffic, and limits how far an attacker can move inside.
tec-ngfw.placement: Network zone. An HA pair at each internet edge (DC and DR), inline between the ISP routers (or the anti-DDoS device) and the DMZ/core switches; a separate internal segmentation firewall pair in the data centre between user, server, payment and management zones; a smaller firewall at each branch.
tec-ngfw.how: Every packet is matched to an application and, where possible, a user. Rules allow only what is needed (default deny) and the allowed traffic is inspected by IPS, anti-malware, URL filtering and TLS decryption. Logs go to the SIEM, and the management console keeps rule history for audits.
pareto: Default-deny rule base, reviewed every 6 months and cleaned once a year
IPS and anti-malware on all internet-facing and inter-zone traffic
Internal segmentation: users cannot reach server or payment zones except through named rules
TLS decryption for user web traffic (with exemptions for banking, health and privacy)
Logs to the SIEM and admin access only from a management network with MFA

tec-email.summary: A filter that checks every email for phishing, malware, fraud and spoofing before (or just after) it reaches the inbox, plus SPF, DKIM and DMARC so others cannot send mail as you.
tec-email.protects: Users' mailboxes and the organisation's domain; stops phishing, credential theft, malicious attachments and links, invoice and CEO fraud (business email compromise) and domain spoofing.
tec-email.placement: Cloud service. Either a secure email gateway in front of the mail system (MX record points to the gateway, which relays clean mail to Microsoft 365/Google/Exchange), or API mode, connected to Microsoft 365/Google Workspace and acting inside the mailbox. Many banks run the native filter plus one of these. DMARC is a DNS setting owned by the messaging team.
tec-email.how: Mail is scored on sender reputation, authentication (SPF/DKIM/DMARC), content, links and attachments. Attachments open in a sandbox and links are rewritten and checked again at click time. Bad mail is blocked or quarantined, and mail already delivered can be pulled back from all inboxes.

Attachment sandboxing and time-of-click link checks
Impersonation and business-email-compromise detection for finance and executives
Automatic removal of a reported phish from every inbox
A report-phish button that feeds the SOC

tec-edr.summary: Software on every laptop and server that blocks malware and records what programs do, so attacks such as ransomware can be stopped and investigated.
tec-edr.protects: Laptops, desktops and servers (Windows, macOS, Linux); stops malware, ransomware, credential dumping, malicious scripts and hands-on-keyboard attackers.
tec-edr.placement: Agent on devices. A lightweight agent on every endpoint and server, managed from a cloud console (or on-premise console where data must stay on site), with alerts sent to the SOC.
tec-edr.how: The agent blocks known and suspicious files and watches process, file, registry and network activity. It flags behaviour that matches attack techniques and can isolate a device from the network with one click or automatically. Analysts search the recorded activity across all devices to find how far an attack spread.

tec-ddos.summary: Protection that absorbs floods of junk traffic so that websites, internet banking, APIs and the internet link stay up during an attack.
tec-ddos.protects: Internet links, public websites, mobile and internet banking, APIs, DNS and VPN gateways; stops volumetric, protocol (state-exhaustion) and application-layer floods.
tec-ddos.placement: Three layers, used together. (1) ISP clean pipe: the ISP scrubs traffic on its backbone before it reaches your link. (2) Cloud scrubbing: traffic is diverted by BGP or DNS to a scrubbing provider and returned clean over a tunnel. (3) On-premise: an appliance inline between the ISP routers and the edge firewall, which handles small and application attacks and signals the cloud for large ones.
tec-ddos.how: Normal traffic is learned as a baseline. When an attack starts, traffic for the target is redirected to scrubbing centres that drop attack packets and pass clean traffic back. Always-on mode scrubs all the time; on-demand mode diverts only during an attack, which is cheaper but slower to react.
pareto: Clean pipe or cloud scrubbing with scrubbing centres in India, sized well above link capacity
Always-on protection for internet banking, payments and DNS
An on-premise device or firewall rules that stop small and application-layer floods and protect firewall session tables
A tested runbook: who calls whom, and a drill at least once a year
Two ISPs, so one attack or outage does not cut you off

tec-dns.summary: A DNS service that refuses to look up known malicious or newly created risky domains, and DNSSEC on your own domains so they cannot be forged.
tec-dns.protects: All users and devices, on and off the network; stops visits to phishing and malware sites, command-and-control calls, DNS tunnelling and data theft over DNS; DNSSEC protects your own domains from spoofed answers.
tec-dns.placement: Cloud service or on-premise. Internal DNS resolvers forward to a protective DNS service (or apply a threat feed locally as a response policy zone); roaming laptops use an agent; branches and guest Wi-Fi point at the same service. Outbound DNS to anything else is blocked at the firewall. The network security team owns it.
tec-dns.how: Every lookup is checked against threat intelligence and categories before an answer is given. Bad lookups are blocked or sent to a warning page and logged with the device and user. Logs show which machine tried to reach a malicious domain, which is often the first sign of an infection.
pareto: All internal resolvers forward only to protective DNS; firewall blocks other outbound DNS (port 53 and known DoH servers)

tec-nac.summary: A gate on the wired and wireless network that lets a device in only after it proves who it is and that it is healthy, and puts guests and unknown devices in a separate zone.
tec-nac.protects: The internal network; stops unknown laptops, rogue devices and infected machines from connecting, and keeps printers, cameras and IoT in their own zones.
tec-nac.placement: Network zone. A NAC policy server cluster (RADIUS) in the DC with a standby at DR; switches and Wi-Fi controllers at every site ask it before opening a port (802.1X, or MAC bypass for devices that cannot do 802.1X).
tec-nac.how: When a device plugs in, the switch asks the NAC server who it is. The server checks a certificate or user login, profiles the device type and, optionally, checks posture (EDR running, patched). It then puts the device in the right VLAN or applies an access list; failed or unknown devices go to a quarantine or guest network.

tec-ztna.summary: Remote access that connects a checked user on a checked device to one named application at a time, instead of putting them on the whole network as a VPN does.
tec-ztna.protects: Internal and private cloud applications; stops attackers with a stolen VPN login from roaming the network, hides apps from the internet, and limits third-party and vendor access.
tec-ztna.placement: Cloud service with connectors. Users run an agent (or use a browser for vendors); small connector VMs sit next to the applications in the DC, DR and cloud and make outbound-only connections to the broker. The security architect owns the design; the network team runs it.
tec-ztna.how: The user signs in through the identity provider with MFA, and the device posture is checked (EDR running, managed, patched). The broker then allows a connection to that one application if policy permits. The application has no inbound port open to the internet; the connector reaches out to the broker.

tec-ndr.summary: Sensors that watch network traffic inside the organisation and alert when something behaves like an attacker, such as scanning, lateral movement or data leaving.
tec-ndr.protects: Data centre and internal networks, including devices that cannot run an agent (IoT, OT, appliances, legacy servers); catches lateral movement, command-and-control, ransomware spreading and data exfiltration that EDR may miss.
tec-ndr.placement: Network zone. Passive sensors fed by SPAN ports or network TAPs at the DC core, the internet edge (inside the firewall), the DR site and key segments such as payment and server zones; cloud sensors read VPC/VNet traffic mirroring or flow logs. Alerts go to the SOC.
tec-ndr.how: Sensors copy traffic (they are not inline), decode protocols and keep metadata. Machine learning and rules flag unusual behaviour, such as a workstation talking to a server it never uses or large uploads at night. Analysts can look back at the recorded metadata, and some tools can block through the firewall or EDR.
